name: Treaty with the Chippewa, 1820 (Treaty of Sault Ste. Marie)
nations: Sault Ste. Marie Band of Chippewa (Anishinaabe), today represented by the Bay Mills Indian Community and the Sault Ste. Marie Tribe of Chippewa Indians
promises: Article 1: the Chippewa ceded sixteen square miles on the St. Mary's River at the falls (Royce Area 112).
Article 2: the Chippewa acknowledged receiving a quantity of goods in full satisfaction.
Article 3: the United States would secure to the Indians a perpetual right of fishing at the falls of St. Mary's and a place of encampment on the ceded tract near the fishing ground.

breaches.what: The Indian Claims Commission found the 10,240 acres ceded were worth $15,000 on March 2, 1821, that the United States paid only goods of nominal value, and that this consideration was unconscionable. It awarded the Sault Ste. Marie Band $15,000.

breaches.quote: the payment by defendant of a nominal consideration for the cession of land worth $15,000 was unconscionable

landTaken: Royce Area 112, sixteen square miles which the Commission found contained 10,240 acres (Docket 18-R, opinion of November 19, 1969).
compensation: The Commission awarded $15,000 in full satisfaction of all claims in Docket 18-R (final award, December 26, 1973).
today: Whether the United States kept the Article 3 fishing and encampment promise was not examined in the decisions opened.

openQuestions: The fate of the Article 3 perpetual fishing right at the falls (the St. Marys canal and locks were built on the rapids from 1853) was not traced to a finding; a deeper pass should look for one and for the Sault Tribe's or Bay Mills' own account.
No nation statement about this treaty was found in this pass.

plain.promised: In return for sixteen square miles at the falls of St. Mary's, the United States promised the Chippewa a perpetual right to fish at the falls and a place to camp near the fishing ground.
plain.happened: The Indian Claims Commission found in 1973 that the 10,240 acres ceded were worth $15,000, that the United States paid only goods of nominal value, and that this was unconscionable.
plain.today: The Commission awarded the Sault Ste. Marie Band $15,000 in 1973. Whether the fishing and camping promise was kept has not been examined.

nationVoice.nation: Sault Ste. Marie Tribe of Chippewa Indians
nationVoice.summary: The Tribe's Story of Our People says that in the 1820 Treaty of Sault Ste. Marie the Anishinaabeg at the Sault ceded 16 square miles along the St. Marys River so the United States could build Fort Brady.
